text:
Once your words are clean, the next thing to do is count them. Take a short text about a fox and a dog. Without its punctuation, it's thirty words. NLTK's FreqDist, short for frequency distribution, tallies every one: thirteen different words, and the word the comes first, eight times. Ask it for the five most common, and you get words with their counts, highest first. And thirteen out of thirty says something too. This text repeats itself.

That ratio, different words over total words, is called lexical diversity. Very, very, very good, good, good, good has two different words in seven. That's zero point two nine. A sentence that never repeats scores a perfect one. But the score falls as a text grows, because common words keep coming back. The first hundred words of Jane Austen's Emma score zero point seven three. The first thousand, zero point four two. Ten thousand, zero point one eight. The whole novel, zero point oh four. So only compare texts of the same length. And a whole novel shows something bigger: the shape of language.

Emma runs to a hundred and sixty-one thousand words, but only about seven thousand different ones. Rank them by count, and the top ten alone make up over a fifth of the book. At the other end, more than two thousand seven hundred words appear just once. They're called hapaxes. That's nearly two in five of the vocabulary. A few giants and a long, thin tail: it's called Zipf's law, and almost every text has it. And the tail never closes. Even Emma's last ten thousand words bring a hundred and eighty-eight it hadn't used before. [curious] So what does the top of the list tell you about the book?
